title: Why Teachers Roll Their Eyes at New CPD Initiatives
author: Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes treats staffroom cynicism about CPD as diagnostic rather than as a character flaw, and sets out six causes with the evidence behind each. Initiative fatigue comes first, with Fullan's observation that constant change without consolidation teaches people to cope by learning not to care. Then the one-off INSET model, which Timperley's work says cannot produce sustained improvement because it is neither ongoing nor connected to classroom practice. Then top-down mandates, which Kennedy's review shows undercut the professional agency effective development depends on. Then generic delivery, where Cordingley's finding that impact is greatest when CPD is subject-specific explains why the A-level physics teacher sitting through a session on engagement strategies disengages. Then bandwidth, and finally the most uncomfortable cause, CPD tied to performance management, which converts development into surveillance and makes resistance self-protective rather than obstinate. The second half is constructive: collaborative dialogic models, practice-embedded application, responsiveness to need, and duration. Her section on buy-in adds credibility as currency, cognitive doorways that reframe resistance as curiosity, and the reminder that culture is the soil rather than the seed.
points: Cynicism is treated as diagnostic rather than as resistance, with six evidenced causes rather than a complaint about attitude.
Fullan's formulation is the sharpest of them, that constant unconsolidated change teaches teachers to cope by learning not to care.
The surveillance cause is the most uncomfortable and the most actionable: CPD tied to performance management makes honest admission of difficulty risky, so resistance becomes self-protective.
The cognitive-doorways technique gives leaders something to say in the moment, converting 'this wouldn't work with our kids' into a question about what a workable version would look like.
Credibility is named as the currency, with the test being whether the person delivering the CPD walks the walk and whether the content is shaped by classroom realities as well as evidence.
quotes: Rather, it is often the result of years of disillusionment of PD which feels irrelevant and out of touch with what they are doing in the classroom, initiative fatigue and a sense that CPD is something done to teachers rather than with them.
Fullan (2007) argues that constant change, without meaningful consolidation, leads to a surface-level engagement where teachers ‘learn to cope by learning not to care.
If teachers can’t see a clear link between what’s being presented and their own needs, it’s little wonder the shutters go down.
When CPD is imposed in a top-down fashion, it often alienates the very people it’s meant to empower.
This creates a compliance culture where professional development is not about developng expertise, but about surveillance.
A session in September, followed by silence until April, is not professional development, it’s a checkbox.
Finally, you can have the best CPD programme in the world, but if your school culture is brittle or risk-averse, it won’t take root.
